course.title: Blockchain Hybrid Course
course.lead: Fourteen ordered days through the blockchain books on this laptop and the four code courses sitting beside them: Mastering Blockchain, the Bitcoin Programming book, the Princeton crypto chapter, the Ethereum/Solidity reference, the Sui Move intro course, the Scrypto challenges, the Cairo book and starklings. Each day names the exact pages, carries a bite of the author's words, and ends at a file you can open and run.
course.method: Same rhythm as the other branches: **recall** the previous days at 1, 3, 7 and 21 lessons back, **read the author** at bite size, **practice** on a real local file, **check** out loud, then pass the mastery gate before the Next button moves.
course.teacher_basis: Lesson fields follow the SyncSenta teacher schema (idea, recall, misconception, check, gate) from Sync-0.0.2/data/ai_curriculum.json.

books.author: Princeton University Press (excerpt, no author line in the file)
books.path: /home/skware/Desktop/blck/Bitcoin and Cryptocurrencies Technologies Princeton University Press.pdf

days.title: Why the double spend was an economics problem, not a coding problem
days.idea: Before blockchain, the hard part of digital money was not encrypting anything; it was getting strangers to agree on one history without a trusted operator. Proof of work buys agreement by making cheating expensive.
days.recall: From memory, say what problem a ledger solves and why a normal database cannot solve it between strangers who do not trust each other.
days.misconception: Thinking blockchain is a smarter database. It is slower and weaker at storage on purpose, because its job is agreement between parties who cannot be trusted, not efficiency.
days.practice: No code today. In your log write a two-column table: for five things a bank does (hold balances, order transactions, reverse fraud, set rules, identify users), name who does it in Bitcoin and whether that party can be refused service. Then list the files you will need later: ../sui-move-intro-course/, ../scrypto-challenges/, ../starklings/, ../cairo-book/.
days.check: Say the sentence 'a blockchain is a payment system that replaces trust with cost' and then give one case where that trade is a bad idea. Both in your log.
days.gate: Explain to a non-technical listener why adding more honest computers does not make a blockchain faster, only more redundant.

days.title: Cryptocurrency fundamentals: hashes, keys, and mining
days.idea: A coin is not a file. Ownership is a signature over a transaction, integrity is a hash chain, and issuance is whoever can present expensive work first.
days.recall: Day 1 (1 lesson back). From memory, name the two cryptographic primitives every cryptocurrency needs and say which one proves ownership.
days.misconception: Believing a coin is stored somewhere, or that mining is searching random numbers for their own sake. The work is only meaningful because the rule set prices it.
days.practice: Run the hash exercise you already have: python3 ../security-exercises/exercises/01_detection/11_hash_integrity.py, then read its solution in ../security-exercises/solutions/01_detection/11_hash_integrity.py. Note in your log how the same SHA-256 chunked loop is what a block header is built from - one more input and the digest moves completely.
days.check: Write, without the page, the difference between hashing and encrypting in one sentence each, and say which one a lost password can be recovered with.
days.gate: Given a transaction that spends the same input twice, say what the network must decide, who decides it, and what stops the loser from replaying it tomorrow.

days.title: The one primitive everything rests on: cryptographic hash functions
days.idea: A hash function is a one-way fingerprint: preimage resistance hides what produced it, second-preimage resistance stops substitution, and collision resistance stops two inputs sharing a fingerprint. Blockchains chain these fingerprints to make history tamper-evident.
days.recall: Name the three resistance properties of a hash function from memory, and say which one MD5 lost.
days.misconception: Calling a hash 'encryption'. Hashing is not reversible and has no key; nothing is decrypted from a digest. Also: MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for collision resistance even though they still look fine for casual checksums.
days.practice: Run python3 and hash the same string twice, then change one character and hash again. Record the two digests in your log and circle every position that changed. Then write down the property you just demonstrated by hand.
days.check: Explain avalanche effect in one sentence and say why it matters when a hash is used as an address.
days.gate: Without notes, describe how a tampered block breaks the chain, and why recomputing the rest of the chain is not enough in a proof-of-work system.

days.title: How Bitcoin works, end to end
days.idea: Blocks are Merkle trees of transactions; a transaction spends previous outputs and creates new ones; the longest-valid chain is the shared history. Unspent transaction outputs, not account balances, are what you own.
days.recall: Day 2 and Day 3 back. Write the UTXO sentence from memory: your balance is the sum of the outputs nobody has spent yet.
days.misconception: Thinking in account balances. Bitcoin has no accounts; there are only outputs and the locks that authorise spending them. That is why privacy, batching and change all behave the way they do.
days.practice: This book is CC BY-SA, so quote it freely in your notes. Read ../scrypto-challenges/README.md and ../sui-move-intro-course/README.md and answer one question in your log for each: which asset model does that chain use, outputs or objects? Both models are UTXO descendants; find the sentence that shows it.
days.check: Draw the transaction lifecycle on paper: create, broadcast, mempool, included, confirmed, spent. Say which steps are reversible.
days.gate: Explain why a change output must be created, and what happens to coins if a wallet forgets to.

days.title: Keys and addresses: the math you actually need
days.idea: A private key is a number, a public key is a curve point derived from it, and an address is a hashed fingerprint of that public key. You reveal the hash, never the key, and a signature proves knowledge without showing anything.
days.recall: Day 4 back. Say the chain: private key, public key, address - and name which two are derived and from what.
days.misconception: Believing an address can be reversed to a public key, or that a wallet stores coins. A wallet stores keys; the chain holds the ledger. Lose the keys and no authority can restore them.
days.practice: Read ../security-exercises/exercises/01_detection/03_redact_secrets.py, then implement it if you have not. Key material is a secret like any other: the same redaction discipline applies to seeds and mnemonics. Write the rule you would use to keep a seed out of logs, screenshots and chat history.
days.check: Say out loud why asymmetric crypto is needed at all when hashing already gives integrity.
days.gate: Explain the difference between signing and encrypting, and say which one a Bitcoin transaction uses and why.

days.title: From payments to programmable state: what Ethereum changed
days.idea: Bitcoin scripts a payment. Ethereum runs arbitrary code over shared state, and pays for that generality with gas: every operation costs because someone must bound the work every node repeats.
days.recall: Day 5 and Day 4 back. State the one sentence that separates Bitcoin from Ethereum.
days.misconception: Thinking a smart contract is an agreement or a legal thing. It is a program at a fixed address whose state anyone can read and whose code nobody can edit after deployment.
days.practice: No toolchain needed yet. Write, in your log, the smallest contract you could actually want: inputs, who can call it, what state it keeps, what it can never do again. Four lines is enough; that page is your Day 7 target.
days.check: Explain in one sentence why gas is refunded for released storage rather than simply being cheaper.
days.gate: Given a bug in a deployed contract, list the three options you have and why each one is expensive.

days.title: Accounts, state and gas: the machine underneath the contract
days.idea: The EVM is a deterministic state machine. Every node recomputes every transaction, so nothing may depend on time, randomness, or the outside world unless an oracle brings it in - and the oracle is then a trust anchor.
days.recall: Day 6, Day 5 and Day 4 back. Say what makes the EVM deterministic and name the one thing that breaks it.
days.misconception: Believing contract code runs on the blockchain. It runs on every node's copy; the chain only stores results. Also: block timestamps are miner-influenceable and are not a clock.
days.practice: Open ../sui-move-intro-course/unit-one/lessons/1_set_up_environment.md and 2_sui_project_structure.md. You do not have to install anything today; write down which parts of a Move package you could not check offline, and keep that list for the day you have a toolchain.
days.check: Name three things a contract cannot do without an outside feed, and say what each would have to trust.
days.gate: Explain why a smart-contract bug is not like a web bug: who can fix it, and how long does the wrong state stay visible?

days.title: Your first contract: writing it, deploying it, calling it
days.idea: Deployment is a transaction that stores bytecode at an address. From then on the only interface is the ABI: function selectors, typed arguments, and events that let the off-chain world notice state changes.
days.recall: Day 7 and Day 6 back. Write the four-step lifecycle of a call: who signs, who executes, who stores, who pays.
days.misconception: Thinking a contract can see your wallet balance or start work on its own. Contracts only react to calls; nothing runs until someone pays to run it.
days.practice: Open ../sui-move-intro-course/unit-one/lessons/3_custom_types_and_abilities.md then do ../sui-move-intro-course/exercises/unit-one/unit-one-exercises.md. Check yourself with unit-one-exercises-answer-key.md only after you have written your own answer, and log the one mistake you repeat.
days.check: Say the difference between a function that is view, payable, or restricted to the owner - and what each guarantees to a caller.
days.gate: Given a contract that mints tokens on a timer, name every party that must stay online for it to keep working.

days.title: Smart contract structure: storage, ownership and upgradeability
days.idea: Storage layout is the contract's real interface. Ownership patterns decide who may change state, and proxy-based upgrades trade the promise of immutable code for a named maintainer.
days.recall: Day 8, Day 7 and Day 6 back. Name the two ways a contract changes and which one is permanent.
days.misconception: Believing 'upgradable' is a technical detail. It silently replaces the claim 'code is law' with 'a key holder is law', and users often cannot see the swap.
days.practice: Open ../sui-move-intro-course/unit-two/lessons/2_ownership.md and 4_object_wrapping.md. Then write, in your log, how Move's ownership model would express the capability check you wrote about on Day 6 - objects instead of a mapping of addresses.
days.check: Explain why storage collisions happen when an implementation contract gains a variable, in one sentence a reviewer would accept.
days.gate: You are auditing a mint function. List the four questions you must answer before calling it safe.

days.title: Tokenize everything: what an asset on a chain actually is
days.idea: A token is a claim recorded in shared state, and its value depends entirely on which claims it can enforce: fungibility, transferability, divisibility, and the right to be redeemed or burned.
days.recall: Day 9, Day 8 and Day 7 back. Say which four properties make a token an asset rather than a receipt.
days.misconception: Assuming a token inherits its chain's security or its issuer's solvency. It inherits neither: a stablecoin is a promise about a bank account you cannot audit in real time.
days.practice: Read ../scrypto-challenges/1-exchanges/CandyDex/README.md then open 1-exchanges/CandyDex/src/lib.rs. Annotate, in your log, which function creates value out of nothing and which function merely moves it. Resource types in Scrypto make the difference visible in the signature; find one line that proves it.
days.check: Name one asset you would not put on a chain and say which property above fails for it.
days.gate: Explain the difference between a token that represents a share and a token that represents a receipt, and what each legally obliges the issuer to do.

days.title: Decentralizing finance: composability and its failure modes
days.idea: Protocols stack because each one exposes state another can read and call. That same openness is the attack surface: price feeds can be manipulated, and any loop that borrows against its own output is a leverage machine.
days.recall: Day 10, Day 9 and Day 8 back. Write the sentence: composability means your protocol's worst input is another protocol's normal output.
days.misconception: Thinking a decentralised exchange settles without counterparty risk. It removes the custodian and adds oracle risk, gas-ordering risk, and liquidity-withdrawal risk.
days.practice: Open ../scrypto-challenges/2-oracles/ and read one oracle challenge README plus one implementation. Answer in your log: who decides the price, how stale is it allowed to be, and what happens to a loan when that decision is wrong?
days.check: Describe one DeFi failure that no code review would catch because every component is individually correct.
days.gate: Design the guard rail you would add to a lending market that prices collateral from a single spot pool.

days.title: Protecting contracts: reentrancy, overflow, and the trust you cannot delete
days.idea: Most classic losses come from three habits: trusting an external call to be harmless, assuming arithmetic is exact, and treating a permission list as a promise. Checks-effects-interactions and explicit amounts are not style rules; they are the only defences a deterministic machine can honour.
days.recall: Day 11, Day 10 and Day 9 back. Name the three habits that cause most losses, with one historic loss class each.
days.misconception: Believing an audit makes a contract safe. An audit bounds your ignorance at one moment; it does not cover the price feed, the upgrade key, or the next caller.
days.practice: Take one finding from Day 11's oracle reading and run it through ../security-exercises/exercises/04_reporting/12_severity_scoring.py, then produce the report with 13_render_report.py. The renderer refuses output without authorization evidence - that is exactly how a contract finding should be written up.
days.check: Say checks-effects-interactions out loud and give the ordering bug it prevents in one sentence.
days.gate: Explain reentrancy to a backend engineer using an analogy that has nothing to do with crypto.

days.title: Catch me if you can: pseudonymity, tracing and what is actually private
days.idea: Public ledgers are transparent to everyone including the analyst. Pseudonymity survives only as long as one identity is never linked to one address, and chain analysis plus coinjoin heuristics plus exchange KYC break that link more often than people expect.
days.recall: Day 12, Day 11 and Day 10 back. State the difference between anonymous and pseudonymous in one sentence.
days.misconception: Thinking a new address is privacy. Reuse, change-output heuristics, and timing correlate addresses faster than cryptography can mix them.
days.practice: Read ../security-exercises/exercises/01_detection/02_failed_login_summary.py and 03_redact_secrets.py again from the privacy side: write the three log fields in your own projects that would let an analyst cluster your wallet activity, and the one control that would stop it.
days.check: Name one legitimate reason a regulator wants chain analysis and one reason that same tool harms ordinary users.
days.gate: Design a payment flow for a clinic that must prove it paid a supplier without revealing which supplier. Say which part needs trust and why.

days.title: Other chains, verifiable compute, and the piece you will build
days.idea: The design space is consensus plus asset model plus execution environment: proof-of-stake for cost, Move and Scrypto for resources and objects, and zero-knowledge systems for proving computation without replaying it.
days.recall: Day 13, Day 12 and Day 11 back. Tabulate Bitcoin, Ethereum, Move, and a ZK system by what each makes impossible.
days.misconception: Chasing the newest chain because it is fast. Throughput claims are made under ideal network conditions and specific transaction shapes; ask what is being counted as confirmed.
days.practice: Choose one and finish it this week, not all three: (a) starklings - work through ../starklings/exercises/intro/intro1.cairo and intro2.cairo, then primitive_types/, reading ../cairo-book/src/ch01-03-proving-a-prime-number.md for why a program can be proved; (b) Move - ../sui-move-intro-course/exercises/unit-four/unit-four-exercises.md with ../sui-move-intro-course/exercises/unit-four/locked_coin_df.move as the reference; (c) Scrypto - read ../scrypto-challenges/3-lending/ and write a one-page design of the smallest component you would contribute.
days.check: Say which of the three tracks you chose and what you can now do that you could not do on Day 1. Evidence: the file path of your work.
days.gate: Explain your capstone choice to someone from Day 1: what does this chain make impossible that Bitcoin allows, and is that trade worth it for your use case?
